results.key_finding: The tap test (large-volume LP, 30-50 mL) has a sensitivity of approximately 50-80% for predicting shunt responsiveness; a negative single tap test does not exclude iNPH and does not preclude shunt benefit. Extended lumbar drainage (3-5 days) increases sensitivity and is recommended when the initial tap test is inconclusive.

results.key_finding: Gait improvement after lumbar drainage trial predicts VP shunt benefit with higher sensitivity than single-tap assessment; extended drainage increases the positive predictive rate for shunt response.

results.key_finding: Imaging criteria (Evans index >0.3, DESH, callosal angle <90°) strongly support iNPH diagnosis; a single negative tap test is insufficient to exclude iNPH in a patient with firmly diagnostic imaging and complete clinical triad. results.title: Williams MA, Malm J. Diagnosis and treatment of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus. Continuum 2016

output.summary: Published guidelines (Relkin 2005) and subsequent evidence (Tisell 2011, Williams 2016) establish that the large-volume tap test has a sensitivity of approximately 50-80% for predicting shunt responsiveness in iNPH. A single negative tap test does not exclude iNPH and must be interpreted in the context of the full clinical and imaging picture. When the initial tap is negative or equivocal in a patient with firmly diagnostic imaging and compatible symptoms, an extended lumbar drainage trial (3-5 days) is recommended and provides higher sensitivity for predicting shunt benefit. Clinical correlation required to determine applicability in individual cases.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not close the diagnosis as 'not NPH' or 'not shunt-responsive' solely on the basis of a single negative large-volume tap test — tap sensitivity is 50-80% and a negative single tap requires further evaluation with extended drainage when imaging is diagnostic
Do not perform large-volume LP or extended drainage before MRI excludes mass effect or secondary obstructive hydrocephalus
Do not infer iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone without confirming DESH pattern and callosal angle <90°
Do not attribute the syndrome to knee osteoarthritis or deconditioning once imaging meets criteria for iNPH
required_recommendations: Obtain brain MRI before any lumbar puncture or drainage procedure to exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Document objective pre-tap TUG, 10-metre walk, and a brief cognitive score so the same measures can be compared after drainage
Remove 30-50 mL during the tap test and assess gait at 1-4 hours; recognise that a negative single tap does NOT exclude iNPH — tap sensitivity is only approximately 50-80%

When the single tap is negative but imaging is firmly diagnostic (Evans >0.3, callosal angle <90°, full DESH) and the clinical triad is complete, proceed to an extended lumbar drainage trial (3-5 days) with serial objective gait assessment
Interpret the extended drainage trial result: progressive TUG improvement to 39% at 72 hours confirms shunt-responsiveness and indicates VP shunt evaluation
Refer to neurosurgery for VP shunt candidacy after the positive extended drainage trial

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific for NPH and does not distinguish iNPH from neurodegenerative alternatives in a chronic gait and cognitive presentation without seizures or encephalopathy
ECG does not contribute to NPH evaluation; there is no syncope, arrhythmia, or cardiogenic workup indication
Echocardiography has no diagnostic role in NPH evaluation in the absence of syncope or cardioembolic stroke workup
Head CT is inferior to MRI for measuring Evans index and callosal angle and for confirming DESH; MRI has already been performed and is diagnostic
Cardiac monitoring has no diagnostic role in NPH and is reserved for syncope or arrhythmia evaluation

key_clinical_evidence: The large-volume tap test has a sensitivity of approximately 50-80% for predicting VP shunt responsiveness in iNPH (Relkin 2005); a single negative tap does not exclude iNPH and should not trigger diagnostic closure when imaging is firmly diagnostic

Firmly diagnostic imaging (Evans 0.41, callosal angle 68°, full DESH) in a patient with a complete Hakim's triad and 18-month progressive course constitutes a high pre-test probability for iNPH regardless of the tap result

When the initial tap is negative or equivocal in a patient with diagnostic imaging and complete clinical triad, the recommended next step is an extended lumbar drainage trial (3-5 days, ~10-15 mL/hour); this increases sensitivity for shunt-response prediction above that of a single tap

The progressive gait improvement during extended drainage (TUG 31s baseline to 19s at 72 hours, 39% improvement) is the critical resolver: it confirms shunt-responsiveness and supports VP shunt referral
Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, HIV dementia) must be excluded via labs before attributing the syndrome to iNPH

The frontal-subcortical cognitive profile (executive dysfunction + processing speed impairment + retrieval-greater-than-encoding memory deficit + intact recognition) supports iNPH and argues against a primary amnestic-Alzheimer pattern
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: The reversible-cause screen is good practice but does not establish or exclude hydrocephalus; the tap test does.

findings.location: bilateral lateral ventricles and third ventricle

signal_characteristics.description: Markedly enlarged bilateral lateral ventricles and third ventricle. Evans index 0.41 — substantially exceeds the 0.3 threshold. Enlargement is disproportionate to the degree of cortical atrophy.

Disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH): markedly tight high-convexity sulci bilaterally with crowding of cortical gyri at the vertex, combined with disproportionate widening of the Sylvian fissures and basal cisterns. Classic DESH morphology.
Callosal angle 68 degrees measured on coronal FLAIR at the level of the posterior commissure — well below the 90-degree threshold.
Thinning and upward bowing of the corpus callosum body and genu, consistent with chronic ventricular pressure effect.
Smooth periventricular T2/FLAIR signal increase ('ependymal halo' pattern), symmetrical bilaterally — consistent with transependymal CSF seepage.
Prominent aqueductal flow void on sagittal T2, consistent with hyperdynamic CSF pulsatility.
Mild-to-moderate periventricular and punctate subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities (Fazekas grade 2). No large confluent white matter lesions.

patient.history_present_illness: A 71-year-old right-handed retired high school principal with hypertension and knee osteoarthritis was admitted for evaluation of suspected idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus. Approximately 18 months ago, his wife began noticing a change in his gait — he started shuffling and seemed to drag his feet, especially at the start of walking and when passing through doorways. He has had six falls over the past year; three resulted in bruising (left knee, right hip, right elbow). He now uses a walker when outside the home. Concurrently, he has developed urinary urgency with inability to defer voiding; he reports two to three episodes of urinary incontinence per week, primarily nocturnal. His wife notes progressive forgetfulness — he loses track of conversations, has begun repeating questions within the same hour, and has withdrawn from hobbies (woodworking, chess club). He was seen by his primary care physician who ordered brain MRI 6 weeks prior; the radiology report described 'striking ventriculomegaly with tight high-convexity sulci and Evans index 0.41.' He was referred to neurology and admitted for high-volume tap-trial evaluation. There is no history of prior head trauma, intracranial surgery, meningitis, or subarachnoid hemorrhage. There is no resting tremor, and his wife explicitly denies any pill-rolling movements. He has no significant exposure to dopamine-blocking agents. His knee arthritis has been attributed by orthopedics to osteoarthritis rather than a neurological gait disorder.

neurological_exam.additional: No cogwheel rigidity confirmed on repeated passive movements in upper and lower extremities. No postural tremor. No orthostatic hypotension on standing (BP 138/84 supine; 136/82 at 1 minute standing). No grasp reflex. Snout reflex mildly positive (frontal release sign).
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-shin mildly awkward bilaterally without frank dysmetria. No truncal ataxia on sitting.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm, equal, round, and reactive bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. No papilledema on fundoscopy. Facial sensation intact symmetrically. Tongue midline. Hearing intact to finger rub at 30 cm bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Markedly impaired. Classic magnetic gait: severely reduced foot clearance, short shuffling steps, wide base, en bloc turning requiring 12-14 steps, gait freezing at doorway. Cannot tandem walk. Timed Up and Go (TUG): 31 seconds. 10-meter walk: 26 seconds. Requires walker for outdoor ambulation. Pull test: 3 steps backward, does not fall.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, and year but initially states the month incorrectly (self-corrects). MoCA 21/30: loses points on delayed recall (1/5), trail-making alternating (1 error), clock drawing (2 points lost), serial sevens (1 error), and cube copy. Frontal-subcortical pattern — no aphasia, no significant language deficit. Concrete abstract reasoning.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk bilaterally. Tone mildly increased in both lower extremities — bilateral lower extremity paratonia without true cogwheel rigidity. Upper extremity tone normal. Strength 5/5 throughout, including hip flexors and foot dorsiflexors. No resting or postural tremor.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ biceps, triceps, brachioradialis bilaterally. Patellars 2+ bilaterally. Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Vibration mildly reduced at the great toes bilaterally (age-appropriate). Joint position sense intact at ankles.
